population: The totals count residents, regardless of citizenship.
gdp: The largest economies, measured in US dollars.
Current-dollar GDP reflects exchange rates and prices as well as output.
internet: How much of the population uses the internet?
The measure counts people who used the internet in the previous three months.
urbanization: Where city living makes up the largest share.
National definitions of urban areas differ, so these percentages need that context.
life-expectancy: Life expectancy at birth, year by year.
These estimates reflect mortality rates in each year, rather than predicting an individual lifespan.
fertility: Births per woman across the years.
This estimate applies each year's age-specific birth rates across a woman's reproductive life.
birth-rate: The denominator includes the whole population, which makes age structure part of the comparison.
ageing: Where older people make up the largest share.
This chart tracks the percentage of residents aged 65 and over.
young-population: Where children make up the largest share.
The chart measures residents aged 0-14 as a percentage of the total population.
working-age: Working-age population includes people outside the labour force.
population-density: People per square kilometre of land.
Small territories feature prominently because the measure divides population by land area.
urban-population: The number of people living in urban areas.
Large populations matter here. National definitions of urban areas also differ.
rural-population: The number of people living in rural areas.
Rural totals can remain large even as the urban share grows.
mobile-subscriptions: Mobile connections counted across the years.
One person can hold several subscriptions, so this does not count unique users.
fixed-broadband: Fixed broadband subscriptions, year by year.
Subscriptions measure connections; households and workplaces can share them.
mobile-density: Why mobile subscriptions can exceed 100 per 100 people.
Multiple SIMs and business subscriptions push this measure above the number of residents.
female-labour: Women aged 15+ working or looking for work.
ILO modelled estimates count both employed women and those available for and seeking work.
trade-openness: Trade as a share of GDP
Imports and exports relative to the size of the economy.
Gross trade flows can exceed GDP, which measures domestic value added.
exports: Goods and services sold abroad, in US dollars.
Current-dollar totals reflect prices and exchange rates as well as trade volumes.
imports: Goods and services bought from abroad, in US dollars.
Current-dollar totals reflect prices and exchange rates as well as trade volumes.
gdp-per-person: GDP per person measures average output. It does not show how income is distributed.
export-share: Exports as a share of GDP
Exports include gross flows, while GDP counts value added. The ratio can exceed 100%.
import-share: Imports as a share of GDP
Imports include gross flows, while GDP counts value added. The ratio can exceed 100%.
industry: This measure includes construction, mining, utilities and manufacturing, in current US dollars.
manufacturing: Manufacturing output after subtracting intermediate inputs.
The chart uses current US dollars, so prices and exchange rates affect the totals.
health-spending: Health spending as a share of GDP
How much of the economy goes to current healthcare spending.
A high spending share alone says little about access, efficiency or health outcomes.
services: The services sector's contribution to output.
The totals use current US dollars and reflect prices and exchange rates.
remittances: Money reaching home through personal remittances.
The World Bank measure combines personal transfers and compensation of employees.
reserves: Current-dollar values can change with gold prices and exchange rates as well as reserve holdings.
unemployment: People without work who are available and looking for it.
ILO modelled estimates measure unemployment as a share of the labour force.
air-travel: Passenger journeys carried by registered airlines.
This airline-based measure differs from the number of passengers passing through a country's airports.
container-ports: Traffic is measured in twenty-foot-equivalent units. A forty-foot container counts as two.
rail-freight: Goods moved by rail, weighted by distance.
A tonne carried 100 kilometres contributes 100 tonne-kilometres to the total.
rail-travel: Rail journeys measured by distance travelled.
Passenger-kilometres count both how many people travel and how far they go.
electricity-access: The share of people with electricity access.
An access connection does not tell us how reliable or affordable the supply is.
clean-cooking: The share of people mainly using clean cooking fuels.
The measure covers cooking fuels and technologies; it excludes kerosene.
renewable-power: The share of electricity generated from renewable sources.
Hydropower counts as renewable here. The chart covers electricity output, not all energy use.
hydropower: How much electricity comes from water.
A high share can reflect a small electricity system, as well as substantial hydro generation.
nuclear-power: The share of electricity generated by nuclear plants.
This compares nuclear's share of electricity output, rather than the number of reactors.
energy-intensity: Energy use per unit of GDP
How much primary energy each unit of output requires.
Higher values mean greater energy use per unit of GDP, measured at 2021 purchasing-power parity.
forest-area: This measures total area. Forest condition and biodiversity need separate measures.
agricultural-land: The measure includes arable land, permanent crops and permanent meadows and pastures.
cereal-production: Total production depends on both the area harvested and the yield per hectare.
coal-electricity: The share of electricity generated from coal.
The chart compares coal's share of electricity output, rather than total coal consumption.
capture-fisheries: Wild fish catches measured in tonnes.
Capture production covers inland and marine catches; farmed production has its own series.
aquaculture: Farmed aquatic production, year by year.
Aquaculture covers cultivated aquatic organisms, including fish, shellfish and aquatic plants.
research-spending: R&D spending as a share of GDP
Research spending relative to the size of the economy.
A high R&D share can coexist with a smaller research budget in absolute terms.
patents: Application counts measure filings, rather than granted patents or the value of inventions.
researchers: The chart compares the number of R&D researchers with population size.
labour-force: People working or available and looking for work.
The labour force includes both employed and unemployed people.
